name: Anthony Nguyen
title: Postdoctoral Scholar
specialties: philosophy of AI; ethics; higher education
bio: He earned his PhD at the University of Southern California. His primary work is in political philosophy, including how the Rawlsian idea of the social bases of self-respect can illuminate colonialism, and he also works in philosophy of language and metaphysics. With Conny Knieling he has developed an account of the moral exploitation of data workers, arguing that the people who label training data and moderate harmful content are wronged precisely in virtue of their capacity for moral judgment rather than despite it. The two have presented the work internationally, including at Seoul National University.

name: Astrit Tola
title: Postdoctoral Scholar
specialties: topological data analysis; graph representation learning; topology-aware AI
bio: He earned his PhD in mathematics at the University of Texas at Dallas in 2025, supervised by Baris Coskunuzer, with a dissertation combining graph representation learning and topological methods. At FSU he leads TopoML&AI, a group building topology-aware approaches meant to make machine learning more interpretable and better grounded in mathematical structure, and collaborates with Malbor Asllani in the mathematics department. His applications range across drug discovery, biological networks, and cybersecurity; a proposal on topological retrieval across cybersecurity knowledge graphs won a ReliaQuest Innovation Challenge Award in 2026.

name: Ben Adcock
title: Professor
specialties: compressed sensing; scientific machine learning; AI stability
bio: He earned his PhD at the University of Cambridge in 2011 in the numerical analysis group under Arieh Iserles, and won the Leslie Fox Prize the same year. NSERC and PIMS fellowships at Simon Fraser University followed, then two years as an assistant professor at Purdue, before he returned to SFU where he is now a full professor. He has held an Alfred P. Sloan Research Fellowship, won the CAIMS/PIMS Early Career Award, and received the Royal Society of Canada's John L. Synge Award in 2025. He has written three books, among them Compressive Imaging: Structure, Sampling, Learning with Anders Hansen, and served as PIMS site director at SFU.

name: Brendon Gutierrez
title: Applied AI Researcher
specialties: Applied AI; Scientific Discovery; Agentic AI
bio: He took a bachelor's in biochemistry at Florida State University alongside minors spanning computer science, mathematics, statistics, physics, astrophysics, and biology, began a PhD in bioinformatics data science at the University of Delaware, and transferred back to FSU in 2025 to continue in computational science. At Delaware he worked in the VIMS Lab on sickle cell retinopathy detection and LiDAR-based fall detection. In Olmo Zavala Romero's PULSE Lab he now builds agentic systems and knowledge graphs for biomedical research, including Synapse, a multi-agent framework for knowledge graph construction, and Mango, a local-first autonomous agent platform.

name: Brian Bartoldson
title: Staff Scientist
specialties: AI safety and security; efficient large-scale neural networks; adversarial robustness and automated red teaming
bio: He is an FSU graduate three times over, holding a doctorate in computational science alongside master's degrees in computational science and in economics. He first arrived at Lawrence Livermore as a summer intern in 2017 and returned as a postdoctoral researcher before joining the staff. His published work runs from the theory of network pruning, where his 2020 paper on the generalization-stability tradeoff is widely cited, through practical training methods such as NEFTune, which showed that adding noise to embeddings improves instruction fine-tuning, to recent work on efficient reinforcement learning for reasoning models. His papers have been cited more than 1,500 times.

name: Christian Hubicki
title: Associate Professor, Director of the Optimal Robotics Lab
specialties: legged robotics; optimal control; bipedal locomotion; biomechanical modeling
bio: He directs the Optimal Robotics Laboratory, where his group designs control algorithms that let legged machines move with something closer to the speed and stability of animals. He studied mechanical engineering at Bucknell University, earned a dual PhD in robotics and mechanical engineering at Oregon State University's Dynamic Robotics Laboratory, and held a postdoctoral fellowship in Georgia Tech's AMBER Lab. He is also among the more visible science communicators in the field: he competed on Survivor: David vs. Goliath, returned for Survivor 50, and is regularly quoted explaining what humanoid robots can and cannot yet do.

name: Conny Knieling
title: Graduate Student
specialties: AI ethics; data labor; moral philosophy
bio: Her work spans general philosophy of science, the philosophy of AI, and the history and philosophy of mathematics. With Anthony Nguyen she has developed an account of what they call moral exploitation: the argument that data workers, the people who label training data and moderate harmful content, are wronged specifically in virtue of their capacity for moral decision-making, and are simultaneously objectified and recognized as moral agents of lesser standing. The two have presented the work internationally, including at Seoul National University.

name: Delaney La Rosa
title: Teaching Professor
specialties: healthcare informatics; AI literacy for nurses; nursing education
bio: Her work centers on healthcare informatics and on preparing both nurses and nursing faculty to use emerging technologies responsibly, covering AI literacy for nurses, professional development for faculty, and the design of equitable, adaptive learning models. She leads accreditation and program evaluation work for the college, including CCNE and state board of nursing reviews, and builds curriculum around outcomes-based assessment and curriculum mapping. Her broader interests include healthcare leadership and the ethical implementation of new technology in nursing practice.

name: Dustin Mixon
title: Associate Professor
specialties: applied harmonic analysis; mathematical signal processing; compressed sensing

name: Eesha Mukherjee
title: Graduate Researcher
specialties: scientific machine learning; medical applications; AI for scientific discovery
bio: She joined Olmo Zavala Romero's PULSE Lab as a doctoral student in 2024, where she works on artificial intelligence and high-performance computing for computational biology and genomic discovery. Her broader interests are in scientific machine learning and its medical applications.

name: Gordon Erlebacher
title: Professor
specialties: neuronal populations; evolving topologies; large language models
bio: He took his bachelor's and master's degrees at the Free University of Brussels before earning his PhD at Columbia University in 1983. Thirteen years in Hampton, Virginia followed, first as a research scientist at NASA Langley and then at the Institute for Computer Applications in Science and Engineering. His work on compressible turbulence from that period, particularly on large-eddy simulation and on dilatational terms, remains his most cited, and he was an early mover in porting scientific simulation onto GPUs. He joined FSU's mathematics department in 1996, became a full professor in 2000, and helped build what is now the Department of Scientific Computing. He directs the Interdisciplinary Data Science program.

name: Hristo Chipilski
title: Assistant Professor
specialties: data assimilation; artificial intelligence; numerical weather prediction; atmospheric dynamics
bio: He read meteorology and climate at the University of Reading before earning his PhD in meteorology at the University of Oklahoma in 2021. He then spent two years at the National Center for Atmospheric Research as an Advanced Study Program Postdoctoral Fellow, a competitive appointment that lets early-career scientists set their own research agenda. His earlier work used ground-based remote sensors to improve how models represent atmospheric convection. He now develops data assimilation methods that draw on machine learning, particularly non-Gaussian ensemble filters for the many cases where the standard assumption of bell-shaped errors breaks down.

name: Jackie Ye
title: Doctoral Candidate
specialties: trustworthy AI; wireless and RF sensing; edge intelligence; secure large language model deployment
bio: They are in the fifth year of a computer science PhD at Florida State University, co-advised by Xin Liu and Shangqian Gao. Their work sits where trustworthy AI meets wireless sensing: systems that perceive and reason about human physical environments without either the privacy cost of cameras or the compute budget of a data center. That thread runs from ARiSE, which makes Wi-Fi-based action recognition cheap enough to run on edge devices, through GeoMotionGPT, which aligns the geometry of human motion with large language models, to MUGEN, which folds motion understanding and generation into a single model. Securing the deployment of large language models is a parallel line of work.

name: Jonathan Adams
title: Professor, Director of the CCI Machine Learning Lab
specialties: AI in higher education; synthetic data for computer vision; RAG for research
bio: His route into computer vision research was an unusually indirect one: a bachelor's in music from the University of Massachusetts Lowell, nine years running a music business, then fifteen years as an interactive software developer at Pilot Media. He returned to study for a master's in instructional design at the University of Massachusetts Boston and a doctorate in curriculum and teaching at Boston University. He now directs the CCI Machine Learning Lab, where the central question is whether synthetic imagery can stand in for real photographs when training computer vision systems. He also holds an FAA Part 107 commercial drone certificate.

name: Jose Miranda
title: Graduate Researcher
specialties: machine learning in oceanography; machine vision; large language models
bio: He has been a doctoral student in Olmo Zavala Romero's PULSE Lab since 2022, developing machine learning methods for operational oceanography in the Gulf of Mexico. His work includes NeSPReSO, which reconstructs subsurface temperature and salinity profiles from remote sensing data, and convolutional approaches to sea surface data assimilation in operational ocean models. He is among the seminar's more frequent contributors, having presented on Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, recent developments in video and audio models, and the economics of a post-AGI labor market.

name: Kathryn
title: Graduate Researcher
specialties: ensemble data assimilation; geoscience

name: Kevin Mueller
title: Doctoral Alumnus
specialties: PyTorch optimization; high-performance computing
bio: He completed his PhD in computational science at Florida State University in spring 2024, supervised by Gordon Erlebacher. His dissertation, "Learning Data-Driven Graphs with Graph Neural Networks for the Classification and Prediction of Alzheimer's Disease", applied graph learning to diagnosis from neuroimaging data. He spoke in this seminar alongside Pankaj Chouhan on getting more out of PyTorch.

name: Kunal Kanawade
title: Graduate Research Assistant
specialties: deep learning; graph neural networks; transformers; diffusion models
bio: He came to scientific machine learning by way of aerospace engineering, with a 2019 master's at Delft University of Technology on algebraic heat-flux modeling for natural convection, followed by work on the stability of hypersonic flows with Datta Gaitonde that appeared in the AIAA Journal. As a doctoral researcher at FSU he works with Nick Dexter on graph neural networks for structural topology optimization and on deep learning for high-dimensional uncertainty quantification. He has given this seminar its sessions on graph neural networks, transformers, and diffusion models.

name: Lan Li
title: Researcher
specialties: future of work; digital labor; online labor platforms; AI and work
bio: She studied computer science at Rice University, took a master's in information studies at the University of Texas at Austin, and earned her PhD in information science at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Before moving into research she worked as a programmer building digital learning tools for students, and she has taught information literacy at university level as well as introductory STEM courses for middle and high school students. Her research examines the future of work, covering digital labor, online labor platforms, and what workplace technology does to the people using it.

name: Max Weinreich
title: Assistant Professor
specialties: algebraic dynamics; billiards; moduli spaces
bio: He earned his PhD at Brown University in 2022 under Joe Silverman, then held an NSF Mathematical Sciences Postdoctoral Fellowship at Harvard, working with Laura DeMarco, before joining Baruch College, CUNY as an assistant professor in fall 2026. His research sits where dynamical systems, algebraic geometry and number theory meet: dynamical degrees, algebraic billiards, and the moduli spaces of pentagons and hexagons. He is also, unusually for someone giving an AI seminar, the author of an essay arguing for total opposition to the use of AI in mathematics.

name: Michael Wolfe
title: Director of AI Research Solutions
specialties: AI for scientific discovery; computational biology; foundation model engineering
bio: He earned a PhD in biochemistry at the University of Michigan in 2019, working with Peter Freddolino on the global interactions of proteins and nucleic acids, and took a master's in bioinformatics alongside it. Funded by an NSF Graduate Research Fellowship, he mapped transcription across the E. coli genome at roughly 41-base-pair resolution and characterized the regulatory reach of Lrp, work published in Cell Systems and the Journal of Bacteriology. A postdoc in Robert Landick's biochemistry lab at UW-Madison followed, and he still maintains open-source sequencing pipelines. He argues that putting AI tools directly into the hands of domain experts, rather than routing the work through intermediaries, is what makes their ethical and accelerated use possible.

name: Nathan Crock
title: AI Engineering Manager
specialties: large language models; retrieval augmented generation; computational reading models
bio: He holds three degrees from Florida State University, a bachelor's in applied and computational mathematics followed by a master's and a 2020 doctorate in computational science, and now manages AI engineering at Premera Blue Cross. He has been a recurring presence in this seminar across several semesters, speaking on large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, and computational models of reading, and returning to agent architectures twice: an introductory session in 2024 and a deep dive the following spring.

name: Nick Dexter
title: Assistant Professor
specialties: neural operators; interpretability; explainable AI
bio: He studied at the Rochester Institute of Technology and worked as an undergraduate research assistant at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the start of a long association: he returned as a research associate before beginning his PhD at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville under Clayton Webster. Four years as a PIMS Postdoctoral Fellow at Simon Fraser University followed, hosted by Ben Adcock, who has also spoken in this series, and he joined FSU in 2022. His research concerns scientific machine learning from limited information, spanning compressed sensing, active learning, operator learning, and approximation theory for problems where every data point is expensive.

name: Olmo Zavala Romero
title: Assistant Professor
specialties: scientific machine learning; oceanography; medical imaging; fine-tuning
bio: He completed his PhD in computational science at Florida State University in 2015 and later returned to the department as faculty. His research splits between two fields that rarely share a room. On the ocean side he has worked with Eric Chassignet on global model studies, including a widely cited 2021 paper tracing where marine litter travels and where it originates; on the medical side he has published on deep learning for prostate MRI segmentation and for automatic contouring in adaptive radiotherapy. He is one of the seminar's most frequent speakers, having covered GenCast, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, transformer fundamentals, and physics-informed learning.

name: Pankaj Chouhan
title: Postdoctoral Research Associate
specialties: PyTorch optimization; tokenization
bio: He completed his PhD in computational science at Florida State University in summer 2024 and stayed on in the department as a postdoctoral research associate, working on machine learning and data science. He has spoken in this seminar twice: once with Kevin Mueller on getting more out of PyTorch, and later on tokenization.

name: Paul Marty
title: Professor
specialties: AI in the classroom; information science; education technology
bio: He came to information science by way of ancient history and computer science engineering, and earned his PhD at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign's School of Information Sciences. Since the mid-1990s he has studied museum informatics, the sociotechnical interactions between people, information, and technology in museums, and he has served on the editorial boards of Museum Management and Curatorship, Museums and the Web, and the Museum Computer Network. At FSU he is Associate Vice Provost for Academic Innovation, and he has chaired committees from the Honors Program Policy Committee to the Innovation Hub Steering Committee.

name: Peter Beerli
title: Professor
specialties: computational biology; population genetics; inference
bio: He earned his PhD in zoology at the University of Zurich in 1994, then spent nearly a decade at the University of Washington in Seattle, moving from postdoc to research assistant professor while working with Joseph Felsenstein, one of the architects of modern phylogenetics. During that period he wrote MIGRATE, a Bayesian package for estimating migration rates and population sizes from genetic data, which he started for the plain reason that no existing software could handle his own datasets. It is still in use and still maintained at FSU, where he now chairs the department.

name: Philippe Miron
title: Principal AI Engineer
specialties: machine learning for earth science; AI automation; retrieval-augmented generation
bio: He is a principal AI engineer at Premera Blue Cross, and before that worked at the weather intelligence company DTN. He keeps adjunct appointments at FSU's Center for Ocean-Atmospheric Prediction Studies and at the University of Miami's Rosenstiel School. His research background is in physical oceanography, covering ocean transport and mixing, vortex dynamics, and geophysical flows, which he has since carried into applied AI, remote sensing, and process automation. His seminar talk on retrieval-augmented generation shipped with a working code repository rather than only slides.

name: Rocío Díaz Martín
title: Assistant Professor
specialties: optimal transport; barycentric coding; applied mathematics
bio: She completed her PhD at the Universidad Nacional de Córdoba in Argentina in 2018, with a dissertation on the spherical Fourier transform on Lie groups, then held a CONICET fellowship at the Argentinian Institute of Mathematics in Buenos Aires. Postdoctoral positions at Vanderbilt University and at Tufts University followed before she joined FSU. Her training is in harmonic analysis, including Fourier analysis, frame theory, and sampling theory, and her recent work carries those tools into optimal transport and its applications to signal analysis and machine learning, with papers at venues including ICLR.

name: Ryan Murray
title: Associate Professor
specialties: calculus of variations; machine learning theory; optimization
bio: He studied mathematics at Brigham Young University, then earned his PhD in mathematical sciences at Carnegie Mellon University in 2016 under Giovanni Leoni and Bob Pego, supported by an NSF PIRE graduate fellowship. He spent three years at Penn State as a Chowla Research Assistant Professor, mentored by Alberto Bressan, before joining NC State. His work brings tools from the calculus of variations and partial differential equations to applied problems across machine learning, optimization, game theory, and materials science. His current NSF grant covers non-local variational problems with applications to data science.

name: Seul Lee
title: Assistant Professor
specialties: AI literacy and ethics; AI education; information bias
bio: She began her studies in South Korea, took a master's in big data in culture and society at King's College London, and completed her PhD in information studies at UCLA in 2025. Her research covers information bias, AI literacy and ethics, human-AI governance, and the assessment of information credibility, with particular attention to how AI education should differ across K-12 classrooms, higher education, and the information workforce. She has recently published on process-oriented AI literacy education grounded in how generative models actually work.

name: Speaker TBA
title: Seminar Speaker
specialties: AI systems; research methods; scientific computing

name: Suvranu De
title: Google Endowed Dean and Professor of Mechanical Engineering
specialties: artificial intelligence and machine learning; virtual reality for healthcare; noninvasive neuroimaging and neuromodulation
bio: He earned his bachelor's at Jadavpur University and a master's at the Indian Institute of Science before completing his doctorate in mechanical engineering at MIT in 2001. He spent two decades at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, where he became the J. Erik Jonsson Distinguished Professor of Engineering, headed the department of mechanical, aerospace and nuclear engineering, and founded the Center for Modeling, Simulation and Imaging in Medicine. He arrived at the FAMU-FSU College of Engineering as dean in 2022. His honors include the American Society of Mechanical Engineers' Edwin F. Church Medal and the J. Tinsley Oden Medal from the U.S. Association for Computational Mechanics, and he is an elected fellow of four professional societies.

name: Tommie Juzek
title: Assistant Professor
specialties: morpho-syntax; natural language processing; large language models
bio: He holds a master's in phonetics from the University of Bonn and a PhD in linguistics from the University of Oxford, and spent several years in the tech industry before returning to academia. He co-organizes this seminar and advises the computational linguistics track in FSU's data science program. His research examines what distinguishes AI-generated language from human writing, why models drift toward particular words, and what that drift does to human language in turn. He built the AI Word Explorer, an interactive tool for examining lexical patterns in large language models, and his findings have been covered by NPR, The Washington Post, and WIRED.

name: Xiaoyang Ming
title: Graduate Researcher
specialties: lexical alignment; large language models
bio: With Tom Juzek he wrote "Fully Automated Identification of Lexical Alignment and Preference-Stage Shifts in Large Language Models", which introduces two measures: a Lexical Alignment Score that detects word overuse, and a Triangulated Preference Shift that estimates how much of that overuse comes from preference learning rather than from pretraining. The method was tested on continuations of PubMed abstracts across six model families, among them Falcon, Gemma, Llama, Mistral, OLMo, and Yi.

name: Xiuwen Liu
title: Professor
specialties: computer vision; pattern recognition; deep learning; machine learning
bio: He began as an assistant lecturer at Tsinghua University, where he had taken his undergraduate degree, then moved to Ohio State University for a master's in geodetic science and surveying and a PhD in computer and information science, completed in 1999 under DeLiang Wang. He joined FSU the following year. His earlier work helped establish spectral histograms as a model for texture discrimination and object recognition, published across IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, Vision Research, and Neural Networks, often with collaborators including Anuj Srivastava and Ulf Grenander. His work at FSU runs through the Florida State Vision Group and the CAVIS computer vision center.

name: Yuri Bizzoni
title: Researcher
specialties: computational criticism; quantitative literary studies
bio: His research applies computational methods to literature, asking whether the qualities readers actually respond to in fiction can be measured at all. He worked on Fabula-NET, a project using deep neural models to assess narrative and literary quality, and his published work covers sentiment analysis, corpus linguistics, canonical literature, and nineteenth-century texts. He teaches computational linguistics and has led courses on quantitative text analysis for humanities scholars, and is currently collaborating on a platform of generative-AI assistants for research.

name: Zina Ward
title: Associate Professor
specialties: large language models; lexical representation; philosophy of AI
bio: She studied economics and philosophy at Williams College, then spent two years at Cambridge on a Herchel Smith Fellowship taking master's degrees in philosophy and in the history and philosophy of science. Her PhD, from the University of Pittsburgh in 2020, is in history and philosophy of science. She works on general philosophy of science and on the philosophy of cognitive science and machine learning, with a book project defending a cluster theory of natural kinds, and has published on neural representation, scientific explanation, and values in science. Her work on why language models overuse words like "delve" reached a wide audience, including a segment on NPR's Science Friday.
